lesson.grammar_point: first conditional with if and unless

listenings.text: Here is the most useful thing I have learned about numbers, and it has nothing to do with numbers. When something falls, most people decide in the first hour, and the first hour is the worst hour to decide anything in. You are not analysing at that point. You are reacting, and reacting feels exactly like thinking, which is the problem. So write the branch down in advance. If it drops below this level, I will do that. If it drops below the next one, I will do this instead. Write it while nothing is happening, because that is the only time your judgement is actually available. A plan with no branch in it is not a plan. It is a hope with a spreadsheet attached.

Hi, about Thursday. Two things could still go wrong and I want us to agree now what we do in each case. First, the client may call it off. He has done that twice and it is nobody's fault. If he calls it off, we send the summary anyway and we ask for fifteen minutes on Monday. Second, the second signature may not arrive in time, and if that happens nothing goes out at all, so we say so on the call rather than promising a date. One favour before Thursday. Please make sure the numbers are in the shared file, so that whatever happens, nobody is looking for a document while the client is waiting. Thanks.

extra_audio.text: Olivia asks whether Thursday is still going to happen. Janderson says Thursday at ten, unless the client calls it off. Olivia asks what they will do if he calls it off. He says they will send the summary anyway and ask for fifteen minutes on Monday. He adds that the client decides nothing without his brother.

reading.rtitle: The Plan B Nobody Writes Down
paras: Every plan has two halves, and only one of them is ever written down. The first half is the meeting on Thursday at ten. The second half is what happens if Thursday at ten does not survive until Thursday, and that half usually lives in somebody's head, where nobody else can see it.

This matters more than it sounds. A plan that exists only in one person's head cannot be checked, cannot be argued with, and cannot be followed by anybody else when that person is on a plane. Writing the branch down takes about one minute and it is the difference between a team and a group of people hoping in parallel.

The branch is also easier to write before anything goes wrong. Once the number has fallen or the client has called it off, you are not analysing any more, you are reacting, and reacting feels exactly like thinking. Everybody who has decided something badly at nine in the morning has felt very clear-headed at the time.

So the useful habit is small. When you make a plan, say the branch out loud in the same breath: if this does not happen, we do that. Worst case, name it. It is usually a delay of two weeks and not the end of anything, and saying that out loud is what turns a setback back into a setback.
reading.source: Article -- a column on planning in a business magazine
